parsed.canonical_question: Why are mitochondria considered semi-autonomous organelles?

render.title: Why mitochondria are semi-autonomous organelles
render.explanation:
Mitochondria occupy an unusual middle ground: they carry their own circular DNA, build their own ribosomes, and divide by binary fission independently of the cell cycle — much like bacteria. Yet the vast majority of the roughly 1,500 proteins found in a human mitochondrion are encoded by nuclear genes, made on cytoplasmic ribosomes, and then imported into the organelle.

The reason goes back to the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria. When an ancestral eukaryotic cell engulfed a free-living aerobic bacterium around 1.5 billion years ago, the bacterium had a complete genome. Over evolutionary time, most of those genes migrated to the host nucleus — a process that is still going on today. Having genes in a single, well-protected nucleus is thought to give the cell better control over protein production. The genes that stayed behind in the mitochondrion (13 protein-coding genes in humans) tend to be highly hydrophobic membrane proteins that would be difficult to import once made in the cytoplasm.

So the paradox resolves like this: mitochondria are semi-autonomous because they inherited a partial genome from their bacterial ancestor, but gene transfer to the nucleus was nearly complete. They can copy their DNA and divide, but they cannot build themselves from scratch — they always need nuclear-encoded proteins to do so. They are more like a very intimate symbiont that can no longer survive outside the cell than a fully independent organism.
summary_bullets: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and ribosomes and divide by binary fission.
Most mitochondrial proteins (~98–99%) are nuclear-encoded and imported after translation in the cytoplasm.
Gene transfer from the original bacterial endosymbiont to the nucleus was nearly complete over evolution.
The ~13 protein-coding genes retained in human mtDNA encode mostly hydrophobic inner-membrane subunits that are hard to import.
This hybrid state — own genome plus nuclear dependence — defines semi-autonomy.
